newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Safety body aims for 20,000 cut in EU road deaths.
newsitem.headline: Safety body aims for 20,000 cut in EU road deaths.

text.p: Random breath tests to detect drivers who have drunk too much alcohol and mandatory speed limits on all major European roads should be among measures used to cut 20,000 from the EU's annual road death toll.

The call for a package of safety initiatives came on Monday from the European Transport Safety Council as it launched a campaign to get EU governments to commit themselves to cutting annual road deaths from 45,000 to 25,000 people by 2005.

"We have come up with suggestions which are realistic. If (EU) member states can sign up to a fatality reduction target -- which they have resisted -- that's going to give the EU work a focus that it has not had so far," ETSC's Jeanne Breen told Reuters by telephone.

The safety lobby group said deaths in road accidents, combined with the 1.5 million people injured, cost EU economies 162 billion European currency units ($190 billion) a year, more than road congestion or environmental damage.

More than half those killed were car users, while those on two-wheeled motor vehicles and pedrestrians each accounted for about 15 percent of deaths. Cyclists made up 6 percent and other road users 8 percent, ETSC said.
Breen said the European Commission, the EU's executive, should use the plan to draw up a comprehensive package of safety measures including the targets.
"Rather than just ad hoc measures one after the other we want an overall strategy to make sure all options are taken up."

Other suggestions included the introduction of safety impact assessments for new trans-European network roads, applying a uniform maximum allowable blood/alcohol level of 0.5 grams/litre for drivers, limiting maximum speeds on major roads to 120 kilometres per hour (75 mph) and increasing seat belt use to 95 percent across the EU.
